title: RC Transients
description: How capacitor voltages charge and discharge exponentially with time constant RC.

study.title: Charging a capacitor
study.body: The switch closes at $t = 0$ and connects a DC source $V_s$ through $R$ to an uncharged capacitor. The capacitor voltage starts at 0 (it cannot jump) and rises exponentially towards $V_s$. The current starts at $V_s/R$ and decays to zero.

study.title: Discharging
study.body: A capacitor charged to $V_i$ that is switched across a resistor $R$ discharges exponentially towards zero, with the same time constant $\tau = RC$. The current is $v_C/R$, so it also decays exponentially.

study.title: The time constant
study.body:
$\tau = RC$ (ohms × farads = seconds) sets the speed of the transient.
- After $1\tau$: 63.2 % of the change has happened (36.8 % remains).
- After $3\tau$: 95 %; after $5\tau$: 99.3 %, so the transient is practically over.
- The initial slope would reach the final value in exactly one $\tau$ if it continued as a straight line.

study.title: Explore: R and C set the speed
study.body: A 10 V source charges $C$ through $R$. Drag either slider: only the product $\tau = RC$ matters, so doubling $R$ has exactly the same effect as doubling $C$. The marked point is always at 63.2 % of $V_s$, one time constant after switching.

study.title: Initial and final value method
study.body:
Every voltage or current in a circuit with one capacitor (and DC sources) has this form:
- $V_i$: value just after switching. Use $v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-)$, found from the DC steady state before switching.
- $V_f$: value long after switching (capacitor open).
- $\tau = R_tC$, with $R_t$ the Thévenin resistance seen by the capacitor (sources zeroed).

study.title: Time to reach a given value
study.body:
Solve the general formula for $t$. For example, charging from 0 to a fraction $p$ of the final value takes $t = -\tau\ln(1-p)$: 50 % at $0.69\tau$, 90 % at $2.3\tau$, 99 % at $4.6\tau$.
**Pitfall:** the ratio inside the logarithm compares distances to the **final** value.

study.title: The current can jump
study.body: Only the capacitor **voltage** is continuous. At the moment the switch closes, the capacitor current jumps from 0 to $(V_s - V_i)/R$, then decays with the same $\tau$. In the charging circuit with $V_i = 0$:

steps.title: Closing the switch
steps.body: The switch closes at $t = 0$. The capacitor starts uncharged, so $v_C(0^+) = 0$. Its voltage then rises exponentially towards $V_s$, quickly at first and more and more slowly as it approaches $V_s$. The speed is set by the **time constant** $\tau = RC$.

steps.prompt: Find the time constant of an RC circuit with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}.
An uncharged capacitor charges through a resistor from a DC source. After one time constant, the capacitor voltage has reached what percentage of its final value?
steps.explanation: $v_C(\tau) = V_s(1 - e^{-1}) = 0.632\,V_s$. The remaining 36.8 % ($e^{-1}$) is what is **left** to go.

steps.title: Try it: the time constant
steps.body: Drag $R$ and $C$. A larger resistance lets less current flow and a larger capacitance needs more charge, so either one slows the charging down. The marked point shows $t = \tau$, where the voltage has reached 63.2 % of $V_s$.

steps.title: One formula for every case
steps.body: Any first-order RC transient moves exponentially from its initial value $V_i$ to its final value $V_f$. Charging from zero is just the case $V_i = 0$, $V_f = V_s$.

steps.prompt: The switch closes at $t = 0$; the capacitor is initially uncharged. Find $v_C$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $\tau = RC$ = {{R|Ω}} × {{C|F}} = {{tau|s}}, so $t/\tau$ = {{t/tau}}. Then $v_C = V_s(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ = {{Vs|V}} × (1 − {{exp(-t/tau)}}) = {{Vs*(1-exp(-t/tau))|V}}.

steps.prompt: Just after the switch closes ($t = 0^+$), an uncharged capacitor behaves like a short circuit.
steps.explanation: True. Its voltage cannot jump, so it is still 0 V at $t = 0^+$: zero voltage while current flows, which is exactly a short. The current is then $V_s/R$.

steps.title: Discharging
steps.body: A capacitor charged to $V_i$ and switched across a resistor discharges towards zero: $V_f = 0$ in the general formula. The time constant is again $RC$.

steps.prompt: The capacitor is charged to {{V0|V}} (+ at the top) and the switch closes at $t = 0$. Find $v_C$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $\tau = RC$ = {{tau|s}}, so $t/\tau$ = {{t/tau}}. Then $v_C = V_ie^{-t/\tau}$ = {{V0|V}} × {{exp(-t/tau)}} = {{V0*exp(-t/tau)|V}}.

steps.prompt: After how long is an RC transient considered practically finished (less than 1 % of the change remaining)?
steps.explanation: The remaining fraction is $e^{-t/\tau}$: $e^{-1}$ = 36.8 %, $e^{-2}$ = 13.5 %, $e^{-5}$ = 0.67 %. Engineers treat $5\tau$ as "done".

steps.prompt: Before the switch closes at $t = 0$, the capacitor holds $v_C(0^-)$ = {{Vi|V}} (+ at the top). Find $v_C$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation:
$V_i$ = {{Vi|V}} (continuity), $V_f = V_s$ = {{Vs|V}} (capacitor open, no current, no drop across $R$), $\tau = RC$ = {{tau|s}}.
$v_C = V_f + (V_i - V_f)e^{-t/\tau}$ = {{Vs}} + ({{Vi}} − {{Vs}}) × {{exp(-t/tau)}} = {{Vs + (Vi-Vs)*exp(-t/tau)|V}}.

steps.prompt: An uncharged capacitor ($C$ = {{C|F}}) charges through $R$ = {{R|Ω}} from a DC source. How long does it take to reach {{p*100}} % of its final voltage?
The capacitor holds $v_C(0^-)$ = {{Vi|V}} and the switch closes at $t = 0$. Find the current $i(0^+)$ just after closing, in the direction shown.
steps.explanation: The capacitor voltage cannot jump, so at $0^+$ it still acts like a {{Vi|V}} source. KVL around the loop: $i(0^+) = \frac{V_s - v_C(0^+)}{R}$ = ({{Vs|V}} − {{Vi|V}}) / {{R|Ω}} = {{(Vs-Vi)/R|A}}. (Before closing the current was 0: the capacitor current **can** jump.)

steps.prompt: The switch closes at $t = 0$. What is the time constant of the capacitor voltage after switching?
steps.explanation: Zero the source (short it) and look into the circuit from the capacitor: $R_1$ and $R_2$ are then in **parallel**. $R_t = R_1 \parallel R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}, so $\tau = R_tC$ = {{par(R1,R2)*C|s}}.

steps.prompt: The switch closes at $t = 0$; the capacitor is initially uncharged. Find $v_C$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation:
$V_i = 0$. Final value (capacitor open): divider, $V_f = V_s\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$ = {{Vf|V}}. $R_t = R_1\parallel R_2$ = {{Rt|Ω}}, $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}.
$v_C = V_f(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ = {{Vf|V}} × (1 − {{exp(-t/tau)}}) = {{Vf*(1-exp(-t/tau))|V}}.

steps.prompt: A {{C|F}} capacitor charged to {{V0|V}} discharges through {{R|Ω}}. How long until its voltage has dropped to {{V1|V}}?
Match each time with how far an RC transient has progressed
Doubling the resistance in an RC circuit halves its time constant.
steps.explanation: False. $\tau = RC$ is proportional to $R$, so doubling $R$ **doubles** $\tau$: the capacitor charges more slowly because less current flows.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the capacitor voltage after a switch closes at $t = 0$. Read the time constant $\tau$ from the graph.
steps.hint: At $t = \tau$ the voltage has reached 63 % of its final value.
steps.explanation: The curve crosses $0.632\,V_f$ = {{0.632*Vs|V}} at $t$ = {{tau|s}}, so $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}. (After $5\tau$ = {{5*tau|s}} the capacitor is practically fully charged.)

steps.prompt: The switch has been **closed** for a long time and **opens** at $t = 0$. Find $v_C$ at $t$ = {{T|s}}.
steps.explanation:
Before $t = 0$ (DC steady state, $C$ open): $v_C(0^-) = V_s\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$ = {{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)|V}}. After opening, the source and $R_1$ are disconnected and $C$ discharges through $R_2$ alone: $\tau = R_2C$ = {{R2*C|s}}, $V_f = 0$.
$v_C$ = {{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)|V}} × $e^{-T/\tau}$ = {{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)|V}} × {{exp(-T/(R2*C))}} = {{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)*exp(-T/(R2*C))|V}}.

steps.prompt: Same circuit: the switch has been closed for a long time and opens at $t = 0$. How much energy is dissipated in $R_2$ from $t = 0$ until the capacitor is fully discharged?
steps.explanation: After opening, the only energy source is the capacitor, and it ends up with $v_C = 0$. So all of its stored energy is turned into heat in $R_2$: $v_C(0) = V_s\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$ = {{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)|V}} and $w = \tfrac12Cv_C^2$ = 0.5 × {{C|F}} × ({{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)|V}})² = {{0.5*C*(Vs*R2/(R1+R2))^2|J}}. The value of $R_2$ only affects how fast this happens.

steps.prompt: The capacitor starts at $v_C(0^-)$ = −{{V0|V}} with the reference + at the top as drawn (so it is initially charged the other way round), and the switch closes at $t = 0$. At what time does $v_C$ pass through zero?
steps.explanation: $V_i$ = −{{V0|V}}, $V_f = V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $\tau = RC$ = {{R*C|s}}. Set $v(t) = 0$: $t = \tau\ln\frac{V_i - V_f}{0 - V_f} = \tau\ln\frac{V_s + V_0}{V_s}$ = {{R*C|s}} × ln({{(Vs+V0)/Vs}}) = {{R*C*ln((Vs+V0)/Vs)|s}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of the initial/final-value method for an RC circuit in order
items: Find $v_C(0^-)$ from the DC steady state before switching
Find $v_C(\infty)$ with the capacitor treated as an open circuit
Find $R_t$ seen by the capacitor and $\tau = R_tC$
steps.explanation: Initial value (before switching, carried across by continuity), final value (after switching, DC steady state), time constant (after switching, sources zeroed), then assemble the exponential.

steps.prompt: An RC series circuit ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}, capacitor initially uncharged) is driven by a pulse: $v_s$ = {{Vs|V}} for 0 < $t$ < {{T1|s}}, and $v_s$ = 0 afterwards (the source then acts as a short). Find $v_C$ at $t$ = {{T1+T2|s}}.
steps.explanation: $\tau = RC$ = {{tau|s}}. Interval 1 (charging from 0): $v_C(T_1) = V_s(1 - e^{-T_1/\tau})$ = {{Vs*(1-exp(-T1/tau))|V}}. Interval 2 (discharging for {{T2|s}}): $v_C = v_C(T_1)\,e^{-T_2/\tau}$ = {{Vs*(1-exp(-T1/tau))|V}} × {{exp(-T2/tau)}} = {{Vs*(1-exp(-T1/tau))*exp(-T2/tau)|V}}. Each interval uses the end of the previous one as its initial value.

steps.prompt: Which change makes a capacitor reach 90 % of its final voltage sooner?
steps.explanation: The time to reach a given **fraction** is $t = -\tau\ln(1-p) = 2.3\,RC$ for 90 %. It only depends on $\tau = RC$, so decreasing $R$ (or $C$) makes it faster. A larger $V_s$ raises the final voltage but does not change the fraction reached at a given time.

steps.prompt: An uncharged capacitor is connected through $R$ to a DC source $V_s$ when a switch closes at $t = 0$. Which graph shows the charging current $i(t)$?
steps.explanation: At $t = 0^+$ the capacitor voltage is still 0 (it cannot jump), so the whole source voltage is across $R$ and $i(0^+) = V_s/R$, the largest value. As $v_C$ rises, the voltage across $R$ shrinks, so $i = (V_s - v_C)/R$ decays exponentially with the same $\tau = RC$ and ends at 0 (in DC steady state the capacitor is an open circuit). The rising curve is $v_C(t)$, not $i(t)$.

steps.prompt: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor from $t = 0$. The graph shows $v_C(t)$.
steps.hint: After one time constant, 36.8 % of the starting voltage is left.

ask.prompt: Read the time constant $\tau$ from the graph.
ask.explanation: During a discharge $v_C = V_0e^{-t/\tau}$, so at $t = \tau$ it has dropped to $0.368\,V_0$ = 0.368 × {{V0}} V = {{0.368*V0|V}}. The curve crosses that level at $t$ = {{tau|s}}, so $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}.

ask.prompt: The capacitance is {{C|F}}. Find the resistance $R$.
ask.explanation: First read $\tau$: the curve drops to $0.368\,V_0$ = {{0.368*V0|V}} at $t = \tau$ = {{tau|s}}. Then $R = \tau/C$ = {{tau|s}} / {{C|F}} = {{tau/C|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: The graph shows a capacitor voltage after a switch operates at $t = 0$. Which expression describes it?
steps.explanation: Read three things: the value just after switching, $V_i$ = {{Vi|V}} (left end of the curve); the final value $V_f$ = {{Vf|V}} (where it levels off); and $\tau$, the time at which 63.2 % of the change is done, i.e. $v_C = V_f + 0.368(V_i - V_f)$ = {{Vf+0.368*(Vi-Vf)|V}}. That happens at $t$ = {{tau|s}}. So $v_C(t) = V_f + (V_i - V_f)e^{-t/\tau}$. ({{tau2|s}} is when only half of the change is done, and $V_f(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ wrongly starts at 0.)

steps.prompt: Two capacitors with the same $C$ charge from a {{Vs|V}} source through different resistors. Curve a (solid) belongs to $R_a$ = {{Ra|Ω}}. Find the resistance $R_b$ of curve b (dashed).
steps.hint: Read both time constants at 63 % of the final voltage.
steps.explanation: Both curves reach 63.2 % of {{Vs|V}}, i.e. {{0.632*Vs|V}}, after one time constant: curve a at $\tau_a$ = {{ta|s}}, curve b at $\tau_b$ = {{tb|s}}. With the same $C$, $\tau = RC$ is proportional to $R$, so $R_b = R_a\,\tau_b/\tau_a$ = {{Ra|Ω}} × {{k}} = {{Ra*k|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: A capacitor charged to {{Vi|V}} is connected through a resistor to a {{Vs|V}} DC source at $t = 0$. Which graph shows $v_C(t)$? (The dashed line marks {{Vs|V}}; the vertical axis is at $t = 0$.)
steps.explanation: The capacitor voltage cannot jump, so $v_C(0^+)$ = {{Vi|V}}. In DC steady state the capacitor is an open circuit, no current flows through $R$, and $v_C$ ends at the source voltage {{Vs|V}}, not at 0. In between it decays exponentially: $v_C(t) = {{Vs}} + {{Vi-Vs}}\,e^{-t/\tau}$ V.

steps.prompt: The capacitor ($C$ = {{C|F}}) starts uncharged and the switch closes at $t = 0$. Choose $R$ so that $v_C$ reaches {{Vx|V}} at $t$ = {{t1|s}} (the orange point).
